learn: Choosing an estimator with the scikit-learn algorithm map
Emerging requirements: fairness, accountability, transparency, privacy, security (FAccT)
Real-world bias cases; COMPAS error-rate disparities; bias in historical data (word embeddings)
Definitions of fairness; why ML models discriminate; fairness through unawareness and the proxy problem; individual fairness and its limits
Need for interpretability; interpretable models (trees, linear regression, k-NN); sparsity with L1 vs L2
intro.why: Responsible deployment requires models that are appropriate, fair and explainable; these considerations increasingly carry legal weight (e.g. rights to explanation and anti-discrimination law) and shape how every model from Modules 1–10 is used in practice.

symbols: false positive / negative rate in group $a$

sections.title: Model guide: the scikit-learn algorithm map
sections.plain: A decision flow from data and task to estimator.
sections.body:
The scikit-learn cheat-sheet routes from START through questions on sample size, task and data type:

> 50 samples?  no → get more data
predicting a category?
   labelled?  yes: < 100K → LinearSVC → (text? NaiveBayes : KNeighbors → SVC / Ensembles)
                   ≥ 100K → SGDClassifier → kernel approximation
              no:  #categories known? yes: < 10K → KMeans → Spectral / GMM ; ≥ 10K → MiniBatchKMeans
                                      no:  < 10K → MeanShift / VBGMM ; else tough luck
predicting a quantity?  < 100K: few features important? Lasso / ElasticNet : Ridge, SVR(linear) → SVR(rbf), Ensembles
                        ≥ 100K → SGDRegressor
just looking?  Randomized PCA → < 10K: Isomap / Spectral embedding → LLE ; else kernel approximation
predicting structure → tough luck

It is a starting heuristic, not a substitute for validation (Module 6).

sections.title: Emerging requirements
sections.body:
• Fairness: ensure gender and ethnic fairness in ML models.
  • Accountability: who takes responsibility for failed ML models?
  • Transparency: make models transparent and compliant with regulations.
  • Privacy: protect user privacy when exposing data to ML models (e.g. differential privacy: outputs change little whether or not any one person's data is included, $P(M(D)\in S)\le e^\varepsilon P(M(D')\in S)$).
  • Security: defend models against data poisoning (malicious training examples that change the learned model).

sections.title: FAccT overview
sections.body: The FAccT field intersects fairness, accountability and transparency, with privacy and robustness, and spans psychology, social science and public policy; statistics and theory; and machine learning. (Covered in more depth in a later elective.)

sections.title: Real-world examples
sections.body: Press reports: an AI hiring tool reportedly penalised résumés containing the word "women's" (it learned from a historically male-dominated applicant pool); laptop face-tracking webcams failed to follow darker-skinned faces (contrast/lighting assumptions); an online passport photo checker rejected an Asian applicant's photo claiming his eyes were closed. Common thread: training data or design assumptions that under-represent some groups.

sections.title: Algorithmic bias: COMPAS
sections.plain: Similar accuracy, different error types by race.
sections.body: COMPAS, a commercial risk-assessment tool, has assessed more than 1 million offenders since 2000, predicting a defendant's risk of a misdemeanour or felony from 137 features. Dressel & Farid (2018) compared it with untrained human judges. The chart shows overall accuracy of roughly 65–68% for both Black and White defendants (humans and COMPAS alike), but false positives (wrongly predicted to reoffend) of about 37–40% for Black vs 26–27% for White defendants, and false negatives of about 29–31% vs 40–48%. Equal accuracy can therefore hide unequal burdens: when base rates differ, a calibrated score cannot also equalise false-positive and false-negative rates (Kleinberg et al.; Chouldechova).

sections.title: Bias in historical data: negative legacy
sections.body: Garg et al. (2018) plot, for many occupations, the gender bias of word embeddings ("women bias", y-axis) against the real difference in women's occupation percentage (x-axis). The relationship is strongly positive: nurse, librarian, housekeeper, dancer high; carpenter, mechanic, engineer low. Models trained on historical text inherit historical inequality ("negative legacy").

sections.title: Fairness: definition and why models discriminate
sections.plain: Absence of bias toward individuals or groups.
sections.body: Fairness is the absence of bias towards an individual or a group (Mehrabi et al., 2019). Can models discriminate? "Aren't machines just following instructions?" ML models approximate patterns in the data, so they learn and can amplify biases at the same time. Common group criteria (not, for reference): demographic parity $P(\hat Y=1\mid A=0)=P(\hat Y=1\mid A=1)$; equalised odds equal TPR and FPR across groups; equal opportunity equal TPR; predictive parity equal precision. They generally cannot all hold at once.

sections.title: Fairness through unawareness
sections.body:
An algorithm achieves fairness through unawareness if none of the sensitive features are directly used. Example: training on Skills and Years of experience only, with "Race and Ethnicity" crossed out:

Race and ethnicitySkillsYears of expHired?
HispanicJavascript1no
HispanicC++5yes
WhiteJava2yes
WhiteC++3yes

sections.title: Issues: sensitive features inferred from proxies
sections.plain: A correlated feature re-introduces the protected one.
sections.body: Sensitive features may still be used, inferred from indirect evidence. Adding "Often goes to Mexican markets" (yes, yes, no, no) reproduces the protected column (Hispanic, Hispanic, White, White) exactly, so a model trained without race can still be a discriminatory ML model. Our synthetic replication (code ex1): with the group removed but a proxy correlated 0.67 with it, the selection-rate ratio between groups only improves from 0.45 to 0.70; dropping the proxy too gives 1.08. Even then, labels from biased history can carry bias through any correlated feature.

sections.title: Limitations of unawareness
sections.body: Fairness through unawareness requires sensitive features to be masked out, which is not easy in real life (faces, names, writing style, pronouns) and is referred to as an individual fairness criterion. Stereotypical vs anti-stereotypical datasets: "The physician hired the secretary because he was overwhelmed with clients" / "…because she was highly recommended" versus the swapped pronouns; models trained on stereotypical data resolve pronouns by stereotype. (Individual fairness in the Dwork et al. sense: similar individuals should receive similar outcomes, $d(f(x),f(x'))\le L\,d(x,x')$.)

sections.title: Need for interpretability
sections.body: Society relies on AI more than ever: autonomous vehicles, security, finance and more. Beneficiaries: end users (enhance trust, understand consequences of decisions, e.g. privacy and fairness); regulatory agencies (compliance, audits, accountability); model designers (diagnose model performance).

sections.title: Interpretability in decision trees
sections.plain: Rules from root to leaf; axis-aligned regions.
sections.body: ML interpretability lets one examine the basis of a model's decisions. The contact-lens tree: tear production rate reduced → none; normal → astigmatism; if no → age (not presbyopic → soft; presbyopic → none); if yes → spectacle prescription (myope → hard; hypermetrope → age: young → hard, not young → none). Each prediction is a readable conjunction of conditions. shows a tree with splits such as $X_2<0.3025$, $X_1<0.8001$ and the corresponding rectangular partition of the $(X_1,X_2)$ plane with leaf probabilities (0.500, 1.000, 0.123, 0.857, 0.333, …). Interpretability degrades as depth grows.

sections.title: Interpretability in linear regression
sections.plain: Each β is a feature's effect.
sections.body:
$$y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\dots+\beta_px_{ip}+\varepsilon_i=\mathbf x_i^T\boldsymbol\beta+\varepsilon_i,\quad i=1,\dots,n$$

The coefficients are the interpretable components: $\beta_j$ is the expected change in $y$ for a one-unit change in $x_j$ holding the others fixed (example plot: "my grumpiness" falls as "my sleep (hours)" rises). Caveats: correlated features make coefficients unstable, and units/scaling affect their magnitude.

sections.title: Interpretability in k-NN
sections.body: A k-NN prediction is explained by the neighbours that voted: the query (star) among Class 1 (green squares) and Class 2 (blue hexagons) is classified by majority within the $k=3$ circle and may change within the $k=5$ circle. Showing the actual similar cases is intuitive (case-based reasoning) but depends on the distance metric and becomes less meaningful in high dimensions.

sections.title: Sparsity for interpretable linear regression
sections.plain: L1 zeros out weights; L2 shrinks.
sections.body:
For $\hat y=w_1x_1+w_2x_2+\dots+w_Nx_N+b$:

$$\text{L1: }Loss=Error(y,\hat y)+\lambda\sum_{i=1}^N|w_i|,\qquad \text{L2: }Loss=Error(y,\hat y)+\lambda\sum_{i=1}^Nw_i^2.$$

The four panels (original coefficients, ordinary least squares, L2, L1) show that OLS and L2 produce many small non-zero coefficients, while L1 recovers a few large spikes close to the original sparse coefficients. Why: the L1 ball has corners on the axes, and the lasso's coordinate update is soft-thresholding, $w_j=\text{sign}(\rho_j)\max(0,|\rho_j|-\lambda)/z_j$, which is exactly zero for weak features. Our run (code ex2): OLS and ridge keep 20 non-zero weights, lasso keeps 3, close to the true (3, −2, 1.5).

sections.title: Interpretability–performance trade-off
sections.plain: Accurate models tend to be opaque; XAI tries for both.
sections.body: Highly performing models tend to be less interpretable. Can powerful models with complex structures be interpretable at the same time ? On MNIST, error rates fell over the years (1994–2012) as models moved from linear classifiers and k-NN to boosted stumps, SVMs and convolutional networks, i.e. from more to less interpretable. Arrieta et al. (2019) place model families on accuracy vs interpretability axes: deep learning, ensembles, SVM, graphical models, k-NN, decision trees, linear/logistic regression, rule-based learning, from most accurate/least interpretable to the reverse, with XAI's future research arena above the curve: hybrid modelling, explainability-preserving modelling, interpretable feature engineering, post-hoc explainability techniques and interpretability-driven designs.

sections.title: Explanation methods, comparisons and misconceptions
sections.body:
MethodTypeScopeNotes
Coefficients / tree rulesIntrinsicGlobalExact for that model
Permutation importancePost-hoc, model-agnosticGlobalDrop in score when a feature is shuffled
Partial dependence / ICEPost-hocGlobal / localMisleading with correlated features
LIMEPost-hoc surrogateLocalFits a sparse linear model around one prediction
SHAPPost-hoc (Shapley values)Local → globalAdditive attributions; TreeSHAP is exact and fast for trees
CounterfactualsPost-hocLocal"Approve if income were 10% higher"
  • "Fairness metrics agree." Demographic parity, equalised odds and calibration conflict when base rates differ; choose based on the harm being prevented.
  • "Debiasing is a one-off fix." Data and populations drift; fairness must be monitored like accuracy.
  • "Interpretability = feature importance." Importance says what is used, not how or whether it is causal.

code.title: Fairness through unawareness with a proxy feature
code.explain: Synthetic hiring data with biased historical labels: compares selection rates when the model sees the protected attribute, only a proxy, or neither.
mistakes: Declaring a model fair because the protected column was dropped.
code.notes: The data are synthetic and illustrative; real audits use held-out data and several fairness metrics.
code.code:
# Fairness through unawareness fails when a proxy feature remains (synthetic hiring data)
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n = 4000
group = rng.integers(0, 2, n)                         # protected attribute (0/1), synthetic
skill = rng.normal(0, 1, n)                           # legitimately job-relevant
proxy = (rng.random(n) < np.where(group == 1, 0.8, 0.15)).astype(int)   # e.g. "often goes to market X": correlated with group
# historical decisions were biased against group 1
hired = (skill + 0.0 * proxy - 1.0 * group + rng.normal(0, 0.7, n) > -0.3).astype(int)

def rates(pred): return [round(float(pred[group == g].mean()), 3) for g in (0, 1)]
def fit(cols, name):
    X = np.c_[tuple(cols)]; m = LogisticRegression().fit(X, hired); p = m.predict(X)
    r = rates(p); acc = (p == hired).mean(); print(f"{name:34s} acc vs history={acc:.3f} selection rate g0={r[0]:.3f} g1={r[1]:.3f}  ratio={r[1]/r[0]:.2f}  coefs={np.round(m.coef_[0], 2)}")
print("historical hiring rates:", rates(hired))
fit([skill, group], "uses protected attribute")
fit([skill, proxy], "unaware (drops it) but keeps proxy")
fit([skill], "skill only")
print("correlation(proxy, group) =", round(np.corrcoef(proxy, group)[0, 1], 2))

code.title: Interpretable models: lasso vs ridge, tree rules, k-NN neighbours
code.explain: Shows L1 recovering 3 true features out of 20, prints a readable tree with export_text, and explains a k-NN prediction by its neighbours.
mistakes: Comparing coefficient sizes without scaling the features.
code.notes: For black-box models, combine permutation importance with SHAP for local explanations.
code.code:
# Interpretable models: L1 sparsity vs L2 shrinkage, readable tree rules, k-NN explanations
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso, Ridge, LinearRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
rng = np.random.default_rng(1); n, d = 120, 20
X = rng.normal(size=(n, d)); w = np.zeros(d); w[[0, 3, 7]] = [3, -2, 1.5]
y = X @ w + rng.normal(0, 0.5, n)
for name, m in [("OLS", LinearRegression()), ("Ridge (L2, a=10)", Ridge(alpha=10)), ("Lasso (L1, a=0.1)", Lasso(alpha=0.1))]:
    c = m.fit(X, y).coef_; print(f"{name:18s} non-zero coefs: {int((np.abs(c) > 1e-6).sum()):2d}  largest: {np.round(c[[0, 3, 7]], 2)}  max |other| = {np.abs(np.delete(c, [0, 3, 7])).max():.3f}")

# Contact-lens style tree: readable rules
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
iris = load_iris(); t = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=0).fit(iris.data, iris.target)
print(export_text(t, feature_names=list(iris.feature_names)))
# k-NN explanation: show the neighbours that voted
knn = KNeighborsClassifier(5).fit(iris.data, iris.target); q = iris.data[[70]]
d, idx = knn.kneighbors(q); print("query class prediction:", iris.target_names[knn.predict(q)[0]], "| neighbours' classes:", [str(iris.target_names[iris.target[i]]) for i in idx[0]])
